newsitem.title: UK: S&P sees strong credit quality for EMU members.
newsitem.headline: S&P sees strong credit quality for EMU members.

text.p: Standard & Poor's said on Monday the credit quality of sovereigns joining European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) was likely to remain strong, and future rating changes will be driven mainly by fiscal factors.
S&P said in a report that it also saw no initial change in ratings for states that do not join the union in 1999.
It said other anticipated effects of EMU included --
- identical euro and foreign currency debt ratings for each government, reflecting the transfer of monetary policy responsibilities to the European Central Bank (ECB),
-- assignment of a triple-A rating to the ECB, like other EU borrowing institutions, and
-- the reduced impact of sovereign credit risk on other issuers based within each state joining EMU.

David Beers, head of Standard & Poor's Sovereign Ratings Group, said ratings of European Union states joining the union in 1999 likely will fall within the triple A and double A categories, similar to their current foreign currency ratings.

"Standard & Poor's believes that nine of the 15 EU member states -- Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Ireland, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands -- should be eligible for EMU membership when the final decision is made in 1998."

Beers said as a result of economic and fiscal differences among the EMU candidates, and their loss of monetary and exchange rate policy flexibility once inside EMU, the focus of S&P's credit analysis is shifting for sovereigns joining EMU.
The main rating factors will be similar to those now emphasised in ratings of regional and local governments --
-- the diversity, performance and prospects of each member state's national economy,
-- intergovernmental fiscal and financial arrangements,
-- trends in operating and total budget balances,
-- debt burdens and contingent liabilities,
-- tax competitiveness within the EU and worldwide, along with tax raising flexibility, and
-- Liquidity and debt management.
"Fiscal analysis, in other words, now will be the dominant criterion for differentiating the credit quality of sovereigns inside EMU," Beers said.
Another important rating factor will be the tax raising flexibility with EMU, especially for states struggling with the most serious public finance imbalances.
"Secession risk could also be a rating consideration."
S&P said this risk is relatively small for the nine strongest EMU candidates, but the same cannot be said for some of the other states aspiring to join."
"Formation of a monetary union with a larger than expected membership in 1999 thus ultimately could call for rating downgrades of the weakest states to deal with this contingency," S&P said.
